title: What can you say about melatonin in your ads and on your site?
summary: The library supports 5 wordings for melatonin; the strongest is "Helps you fall asleep faster when sleeplessness is occasional" (strong, 0.1-10 mg a day). Avoid wording that names or implies a disease, a drug or a treatment, such as "Treats insomnia".

supported_wordings.wording: Helps you fall asleep faster when sleeplessness is occasional.
supported_wordings.why: Authorized in the EU after EFSA review at 1 mg, and listed by Health Canada at a range that includes 1 mg.
supported_wordings.dose_details: EU: 1 mg taken close to bedtime, and the consumer is told so. Health Canada: 0.1-10 mg a day, taken 30-60 minutes before bedtime, for adults 18 and older who fall asleep slowly. The two sources agree at about 1 mg.

sources.name: Commission Regulation (EU) No 432/2012, list of permitted health claims

supported_wordings.wording: Helps ease jet lag, such as daytime tiredness and disturbed sleep.
supported_wordings.why: Authorized in the EU after EFSA review and listed by Health Canada at overlapping doses.
supported_wordings.dose_details: EU: at least 0.5 mg taken close to bedtime on the first day of travel and the following few days. Health Canada: 0.5-10 mg a day, 30-60 minutes before bedtime, adults 18 and older.

sources.name: Commission Regulation (EU) No 432/2012, list of permitted health claims

supported_wordings.wording: Helps reset the body's sleep-wake cycle.
supported_wordings.why: Health Canada lists it; no other listed source covers this wording.
supported_wordings.dose_details: Adults 18 and older, 30-60 minutes before bedtime.

supported_wordings.wording: Helps increase total sleep time when sleep is cut short or the sleep schedule shifts, as with shift work or jet lag.
supported_wordings.why: Health Canada lists it; no other listed source covers this wording.
supported_wordings.dose_details: Adults 18 and older, 30-60 minutes before bedtime.

supported_wordings.why: Health Canada lists it; the EU's narrower claim covers falling asleep faster, not sleep in general.
supported_wordings.dose_details: Adults 18 and older, taken as needed 30-60 minutes before bedtime.

wordings_to_avoid.why: Insomnia is a diagnosable sleep disorder; the supported wording is about falling asleep faster and the sleep-wake cycle.

wordings_to_avoid.wording: Treats delayed sleep phase disorder, or other sleep disorders
wordings_to_avoid.why: Names a disorder. Health Canada's own wording mentions people with delayed sleep phase disorder, but in a disease-claim review that names a disease.

wordings_to_avoid.wording: A drug-free sleeping pill, or works like a prescription sleep medicine
wordings_to_avoid.why: Compares the product to a drug.

wordings_to_avoid.wording: Helps you fall asleep if you have difficulty falling asleep
wordings_to_avoid.why: FDA's 2000 rule (page 1031) says this implies treating insomnia unless the context makes clear the product is only for occasional sleeplessness.
FDA's 2000 rule (page 1031) says help falling asleep implies treating insomnia unless the context makes clear the product is only for occasional sleeplessness.

evidence_strengths.strong: At least two listed sources support it independently at a comparable dose and form, and none disagrees.
evidence_strengths.moderate: One listed source supports it as an evidence-based use at that dose, and no listed source disagrees.
evidence_strengths.limited: The only support is traditional use, the sources disagree, or the source itself calls the evidence weak.

reasons_to_avoid.drug: names a drug or presents the product as one
reasons_to_avoid.treatment: promises to treat, cure or prevent a condition

sources.name: Commission Regulation (EU) No 432/2012, list of permitted health claims
FDA final rule on structure/function statements, 65 FR 1000 (6 January 2000), page 1031

disclaimer: Not legal advice. This guide shows the wording that published evidence supports at a daily dose, from the sources linked below; it is not a ruling on any claim. Your own product, its form and dose, and your own evidence still need to match the wording you use.
